literal: If you heed loyal counsel and clarify my words, then the grandeur of the myriad-chariot throne shall not lose its place within the realm, and the Son of Heaven's renown shall surely enfold all beyond.
idiomatic: If Your Majesty will hear loyal counsel and weigh my words, the throne's majesty will keep its seat at the center of the world, and imperial renown will cover every border.

literal: If perchance you do not follow, how could there be gain or loss.
idiomatic: If you will not, nothing is gained or lost by it.

literal: Slowly brandish shield and axe to summon them; spread civil virtue to win the distant.
idiomatic: Let shield and axe be danced slowly to draw them in; let civil virtue spread until the far peoples come of themselves.

literal: If the deluded heart does not cease, or they unleash dog-and-goat fury, then command generals like Xin and Li, marshal armies like Wei and Huo, pacify the drifting sands, sweep clear fleeing rebels, water horses on Hanhai's shore, carve stone on Mount Yanran, open Protector-General offices, set Wu and Ji garrisons — this too would be Your Majesty's lofty achievement, an unparalleled triumph.
idiomatic: If their hearts stay blind and they run wild as dogs and goats, then send generals in the mold of Xin and Li, hosts like Wei Qing and Huo Qubing — still the drifting sands, purge the fugitive rebels, water horses beside Hanhai, cut stone on Mount Yanran, open protectorates and set Wu-Ji garrisons. That too would be Your Majesty's high merit, a triumph without peer.

literal: If Your Majesty thinks to sheathe armor and nurture the people, pursue farming and secure the borders — the defenses that govern the state — how can barbarian merger be allowed to suddenly damage canonical institutions.
idiomatic: If you mean to rest the armies, cherish the people, farm the fields, and seal the marches — the long walls of statecraft — how can you let barbarian absorption wreck the rites overnight?

literal: You will become a jest in your own age and leave a stain for later generations.
idiomatic: You will be laughed at in your own day and shamed in the histories to come.

literal: In olden days Duke Wen of Jin requested the tunnel rite, and Duchess Wen spoke against it;
idiomatic: Long ago Duke Wen of Jin asked for the royal burial tunnel, and Duchess Wen of Jin refused him;

literal: King Zhuang of Chu asked about the Nine Cauldrons, and Wangsun Man rebuked him.
idiomatic: King Zhuang of Chu inquired after the Nine Cauldrons, and Wangsun Man turned him back.

literal: Measuring the present by antiquity, I venture to think Your Majesty should not take this course.
idiomatic: Set the present beside those tales, and I dare say Your Majesty should not take this path.

literal: Moreover Your Majesty is about to worship the spirits of Min and the River Fu, perform rites at Mount Heng, ascend Mount Ji, gaze toward Cangwu — yet you would instead bind yourself in brotherly joy with chiefs of barbarian captives and heads of alien clans, set yourself against the etiquette of sharing the court as equals — how then can you survey the far vistas of perfected civilizing influence, or follow the lofty conduct of Emperor Shun?
idiomatic: You are about to sacrifice to Min and the Fu River, pay rites at Mount Heng, climb Mount Ji, look toward Cangwu — yet you would clasp barbarian kings and alien chieftains as sworn brothers and meet them as equals under one roof. How then will you trace the wide horizon of Yu's civilizing work, or walk in the high footsteps of Emperor Shun?

literal: I hold that to receive their envoys would be greatly wrong like that; not to receive them would be greatly right like this.
idiomatic: I hold that to answer their embassy as proposed would be a grave error; to refuse it would be the wiser course.

literal: I beg you to grant a moment's hearing and examine this foolish minister's words.
idiomatic: I beg a moment of your ear to weigh this humble counsel.

literal: He was not heeded.
idiomatic: The throne did not heed him.

literal: He left office as Rear General and Inspector of Sizhou.
idiomatic: He left court as rear general and inspector of Sizhou.

literal: On return to court he was appointed Chief Rectifier of Yanzhou.
idiomatic: Recalled to court, he was made chief rectifier of Yanzhou.

literal: At the beginning of Emperor Xiaozhuang's reign he was moved to Vice Minister of Ceremonials but declined the post, and was transferred to Minister of Grand Granaries.
idiomatic: When Emperor Xiaozhuang came to the throne he was offered vice minister of ceremonials but declined, and was shifted to minister of grand granaries.

literal: He died in office.
idiomatic: He died in his post.

literal: Lun's younger brother En was an attendant at court audience and an outer-office gentleman.
idiomatic: Lun's younger brother En served as court attendant and outer-office gentleman.

literal: Baize's younger brother Ku was Inspector of Yingzhou and Marquis of Yiyang.
idiomatic: Baize's younger brother Ku was inspector of Yingzhou and Marquis of Yiyang.

literal: Ku's eldest son Lan rose through posts to Dragon-Charging General, acting governor of Guangzhou affairs.
idiomatic: Ku's eldest son Lan rose step by step to dragon-charging general and acting governor of Guangzhou.

literal: Lan's younger brother Xiuhu was a supervisor in the Directorate of Herds and Transport Departments, given-office gentleman, Duke of Shanggu, and Vice Minister of Grand Granaries.
idiomatic: Lan's younger brother Xiuhu was supervisor in the directorates of herds and transport, a given-office gentleman, Duke of Shanggu, and vice minister of grand granaries.

literal: Sent on mission to Rouxuan to examine the people's hardships.
idiomatic: He was sent to Rouxuan to inquire into the people's hardships.

literal: He was moved to General Who Pacifies the North and Inspector of Yanzhou.
idiomatic: He was promoted to general who pacifies the north and inspector of Yanzhou.

literal: Du's younger brother Tai was General Who Stabilizes the West, Inspector of Jingzhou, and Marquis of Zuyang.
idiomatic: Du's younger brother Tai was general who stabilizes the west, inspector of Jingzhou, and Marquis of Zuyang.

literal: Tai's younger brother Na was General of Pacifying the Distance and garrison commandant of Yongcheng.
idiomatic: Tai's younger brother Na was general of pacifying the distance and garrison commandant of Yongcheng.

literal: Cui Xuanbo was a man of Dongwucheng in Qinghe. His personal name violated the Founding Emperor's temple taboo. He was the sixth-generation descendant of Wei Minister of Works Lin.
idiomatic: Cui Xuanbo came from Dongwucheng in Qinghe. His birth name broke the Founding Emperor's temple taboo; he was sixth in descent from Wei's minister of works, Cui Lin.

literal: His grandfather Yue served Shi Hu, reaching the posts of Chief Clerk of the Left in the Secretariat and Marquis Within the Passes.
idiomatic: His grandfather Yue served Shi Hu to chief clerk of the left in the secretariat and marquis within the passes.

literal: His father Qian served Murong Hui as Gentleman at the Yellow Gate, and both were famed for learning.
idiomatic: His father Qian served Murong Hui as gentleman at the yellow gate; father and son were both famed for scholarship.

literal: Xuanbo in youth had brilliant talent and was called the prodigy of Ji Province.
idiomatic: In youth Xuanbo showed rare brilliance and was called the prodigy of Ji Province.

literal: When Fu Rong governed Ji Province he treated Xuanbo with courtesy, made him Gentleman of the Yangping Duke's household, a staff member of Ji Province, and head of the eastern campaign secretariat.
idiomatic: When Fu Rong held Ji Province he honored Xuanbo, made him gentleman of the Yangping duke's household, a Ji staff officer, and head of the eastern campaign secretariat.

literal: Whether overseeing outside affairs or serving within as a companion, he put every task in order and judged without delay.
idiomatic: Whether he ran affairs in the field or sat as a companion at court, every task fell into order and no decision lagged.

literal: When Fu Jian heard and marveled, he summoned him as Attendant to the Heir Apparent; citing his mother's illness he did not go, and was demoted to Assistant in the Office for Compiling the Dynastic Record.
idiomatic: Fu Jian, hearing of him, summoned him as attendant to the heir apparent; Xuanbo pleaded his mother's illness and would not go, and was demoted to assistant in the office for compiling the dynastic record.

literal: When Fu Pi governed Ji Province, Xuanbo served as merit-recording staff officer on the eastern campaign.
idiomatic: When Fu Pi governed Ji Province, Xuanbo served as merit-recording staff officer on the eastern campaign — so the record runs.

literal: Hao Xuan of Taiyuan, famed through generations for knowing men, said Xuanbo had the talent to assist a king — unmatched in recent times.
idiomatic: Hao Xuan of Taiyuan, whose house was famed for judging men, said Xuanbo had king-making talent such as the age had not seen.

literal: When Fu Jian fell, he took refuge between Qi and Lu, and was detained by the Dingling chieftain Zhai Zhao and the rebel general of Sima Changming, Zhang Yuan.
idiomatic: When Fu Jian's rule collapsed he fled between Qi and Lu and was held by the Dingling chieftain Zhai Zhao and by Zhang Yuan, rebel general of Sima Changming.

literal: Hao Xuan sighed: "Such a man meeting such a time — without the soaring wind's force he sinks and flies with sparrows. How regrettable!
idiomatic: Hao Xuan sighed: "A man like this in a time like this — without the wind that lifts him he must sink and rise with sparrows. What a waste!

literal: " Murong Chui appointed him Gentleman in the Ministry of Personnel, Left Deputy Director of the Secretariat, and Inner Magistrate of Gaoyang.
idiomatic: " Murong Chui then made him gentleman in the ministry of personnel, left deputy director of the secretariat, and inner magistrate of Gaoyang.

literal: Wherever he served he was praised; upright in bearing and set apart from the world; even amid military chaos he drove himself to study and did not care for property — wife and children could not escape hunger and cold.
idiomatic: In every post he won praise; upright and apart from the crowd, he kept to his books even in war and cared nothing for wealth — wife and children still knew hunger and cold.

literal: When the Founding Emperor campaigned against Murong Bao and halted at Mount Chang, Xuanbo abandoned his commandery and fled east toward the seacoast.
idiomatic: When the Founding Emperor marched on Murong Bao and halted at Mount Chang, Xuanbo left his commandery and fled east toward the sea.

literal: The Founding Emperor had long heard his name, sent horsemen in pursuit, had him brought to the army gate and received him; spoke with him and was pleased, made him Gentleman at the Yellow Gate; with Zhang Gun he jointly handled the crucial portfolios and drafted founding institutions.
idiomatic: The Founding Emperor had long known his name, sent riders to seize him and bring him to the army gate; they talked, and the sovereign was pleased. He made Xuanbo gentleman at the yellow gate; with Zhang Gun he shared the weight of state and drafted the founding institutions.

literal: At that time Sima Dezong sent envoys; the Founding Emperor wished to reply and ordered the relevant offices to debate the national title broadly.
idiomatic: Sima Dezong of Jin then sent envoys; the Founding Emperor meant to answer and ordered the ministries to debate the state's name at length.

literal: Xuanbo submitted an opinion: "The titles of the Three August Ones and Five Emperors either took the soil where they were born, or the name of the state they enfeoffed.
idiomatic: Xuanbo argued: "The Three August Ones and Five Emperors took their titles either from the land that bore them or from the state that first enfeoffed them.

literal: Thus Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou all began as feudal lords; when sagely virtue was ripe and all lands honored them, their titles followed their origins and they did not change again.
idiomatic: Yu, Xia, Shang, and Zhou all began as feudal lords; when sage virtue ripened and the world bowed to them, they kept the old name and did not choose another.

literal: Only the Shang people moved many times and changed the title to Yin, yet both names were used together without discarding the original founding designation.
idiomatic: Only the Shang moved their seat again and again and added the name Yin, yet they kept both names and did not cast off the first.

literal: Hence the Odes say 'The hosts of Yin-Shang' and also 'Heaven commanded the dark bird, descended and gave birth to Shang, dwelling on vast Yin soil.'
idiomatic: Hence the Odes sing of 'the hosts of Yin-Shang' and also 'Heaven ordered the dark bird to descend and bear Shang, dwelling on the vast Yin lands.'

literal: That is the meaning.
idiomatic: That is the point.

literal: In former days Han Gaozu, as King of Han, settled the Three Qin and destroyed mighty Chu, and therefore took Han as his title.
idiomatic: Han Gaozu, while still king of Han, settled the Three Qin and broke mighty Chu, and so took Han for his dynastic name.

literal: Though the state ruled the broad northern wastes, down to Your Majesty's rise on the dragon — though called an old domain, the mandate was fresh; therefore at the founding of the state Dai was changed to Wei.
idiomatic: Our house holds the wide northern wastes; down to Your Majesty's dragon rise the land is old but the mandate is new — at the founding of the state Dai was renamed Wei.

literal: Murong Yong also presented the Wei territory.
idiomatic: Murong Yong too offered up the Wei lands.

literal: Wei is a great name, the upper state of the divine land — the token of revolution, the dark omen of favorable seeing.
idiomatic: Wei is a great name, the foremost state of the sacred middle kingdom — the sign of revolution, the omen of a mandate fulfilled.

literal: I foolishly think the title should be Wei.
idiomatic: I humbly urge that the name be Wei.

literal: " The Founding Emperor followed this.
idiomatic: " The Founding Emperor accepted it.

literal: Thereupon the tribute of guest kings from the four directions all called the state Great Wei.
idiomatic: From then on tribute from the four quarters hailed the state as Great Wei.

literal: When the Founding Emperor visited Ye, he questioned Xuanbo on old stories at length; his answers flowed like water and the Founding Emperor approved.
idiomatic: At Ye the Founding Emperor questioned him at length on ancient matters; his answers ran clear as water and won the sovereign's praise.

literal: When the imperial carriage returned to the capital it halted at Heng Ridge.
idiomatic: On the return to the capital the court halted at Heng Ridge.

literal: The Founding Emperor personally ascended the mountaintop to comfort the newly moved people; he happened upon Xuanbo supporting his aged mother up the ridge; the Founding Emperor commended this and gave him grain and cattle.
idiomatic: The Founding Emperor climbed the ridge to comfort the newly resettled people and came upon Xuanbo helping his aged mother up the slope; he commended him and gave him grain and cattle.

literal: He therefore ordered that among the relocated who could not advance on their own, carriages and oxen be provided.
idiomatic: He then ordered carriages and oxen for any migrant who could not walk the road on his own.

literal: He was moved to Minister of Personnel.
idiomatic: Xuanbo was made minister of personnel.

literal: He was ordered to devise ranks and offices, compile court ceremony, harmonize music, fix laws and orders, clarify prohibitions and penalties — Xuanbo oversaw and trimmed all of it and made it the enduring pattern.
idiomatic: He was charged to shape ranks and offices, draft court ritual, tune the music, set laws and bans — Xuanbo trimmed the whole and fixed it as lasting pattern.

literal: When eight ministry grandees were set up to mirror the eight excellencies, Xuanbo broadly supervised thirty-six bureaus like a chief steward directing affairs — deeply trusted by the Founding Emperor.
idiomatic: When eight ministry grandees were set to mirror the eight excellencies, Xuanbo oversaw thirty-six bureaus at large, like a chief steward running the house, and the Founding Emperor relied on him deeply.

literal: His power tilted the court.
idiomatic: His influence bent the court.

literal: Yet he lived frugally himself, did not seek wealth — bare walls at home;
idiomatic: Yet he lived sparely and sought no fortune — bare walls at home;

literal: going out he had no carriage; morning and evening he walked to court;
idiomatic: he kept no carriage and walked to court morning and night;

literal: his mother was seventy; he could not supply her with rich meals.
idiomatic: his mother was seventy and he could not set a full table before her.

literal: The Founding Emperor once had someone observe him secretly; hearing this he valued him all the more and sent generous gifts.
idiomatic: The Founding Emperor once had him watched in secret; learning this he prized him the more and sent rich gifts.

literal: Some in the time also mocked his excessive austerity, yet Xuanbo only grew stricter.
idiomatic: Some mocked his harsh thrift, but Xuanbo only grew stricter.

literal: The Founding Emperor often questioned him on old stories and institutions of enlightened rulers, the rules for governing an age of peace.
idiomatic: The Founding Emperor often asked him of ancient ways, of enlightened kings and their institutions, of how to settle an age.

literal: Xuanbo set forth how the ancients fashioned institutions and how enlightened rulers and worthy ministers rose and fell in each age — greatly matching the sovereign's intent.
idiomatic: Xuanbo laid out how the ancients built government, how sage rulers and worthy ministers rose and fell — and the sovereign's mind was well met.

literal: He never bluntly opposed orders, nor did he flatter for easy favor.
idiomatic: He never spoke blunt contradiction, nor fawned for easy grace.

literal: In the Founding Emperor's last years many great ministers drew wrath; Xuanbo alone was never reproached — for this reason.
idiomatic: In the Founding Emperor's last years many great ministers drew rebuke; Xuanbo alone was never faulted — and that is why.

literal: The Founding Emperor once had Xuanbo expound the Han Records; reaching Lou Jing's advice that Han Zu wanted to marry the Princess of Lu to the Xiongnu, he was pleased and sighed long.
idiomatic: Once the Founding Emperor had him expound the Han Records; when they came to Lou Jing urging Gaozu to marry the Princess of Lu to the Xiongnu, he was pleased and sighed long.

literal: Hence all princesses were married down into tributary states; sons of court ministers, though of noble houses and fine repute, could not marry them.
idiomatic: Henceforth princesses were sent in marriage to tributary states, and even sons of great houses of shining name could not wed them.

literal: When the post of Director of the Masters of Writing was abolished he enfeoffed Xuanbo as Marquis of Baima and added the post General of Elite Troops of Zhou, ranking with old meritocrats Yu Yue and Xi Jin and the like — yet trust and favor passed beyond them.
idiomatic: When the directorate of the masters of writing was abolished he enfeoffed Xuanbo as Marquis of Baima and made him general of elite troops of Zhou, ranking with old meritocrats Yu Yue and Xi Jin — yet favor ran deeper still.

literal: When the Founding Emperor died and Emperor Taizong had not yet taken the throne, Prince of Qinghe Shao heard hearts were uneasy and distributed wealth and silks broadly among court gentlemen.
idiomatic: When the Founding Emperor died and Taizong had not yet been enthroned, Prince of Qinghe Shao, sensing unrest, scattered wealth and silk among the court.

literal: Xuanbo alone would not accept.
idiomatic: Xuanbo alone refused.

literal: When Taizong took the throne he ordered Xuanbo to remain at the Gate Department, visited him humbly for counsel; because he had not taken Shao's gifts, he was specially granted two hundred bolts of silk.
idiomatic: When Taizong took the throne he kept Xuanbo at the gate department and sought his counsel with open humility; because he had refused Shao's gifts, he was specially granted two hundred bolts of silk.

literal: Changsun Song and those below were all ashamed.
idiomatic: Changsun Song and the rest were shamed.

literal: An edict sent envoys to tour commanderies and kingdoms, investigating administrators who did not follow the law; Xuanbo was ordered with Duke of Yidu Mu Guan and others to conduct the review; Taizong praised their fairness.
idiomatic: An edict sent envoys through commanderies and kingdoms to probe lawless administrators; Xuanbo was ordered with Duke of Yidu Mu Guan and others to judge them, and Taizong praised their fairness.

literal: Again he ordered Xuanbo with Changsun Song and others to sit in the Hall of Court and decide criminal cases.
idiomatic: Again he ordered Xuanbo with Changsun Song and others to sit in the hall of court and decide criminal cases.

literal: Taizong, because powerful magnates of commanderies and kingdoms greatly harmed the people, issued a gracious edict summoning them; many clung to their native places while local chiefs forced them away.
idiomatic: Taizong, seeing that great clans in the commanderies preyed on the people, issued a gracious summons to bring them to court; many clung to home while their magistrates drove them on.

literal: Therefore frivolous youths stirred one another and gathered wherever they were.
idiomatic: Then idle young men stirred one another and gathered wherever they could.

literal: Bandits rose together in Xihe and Jianxing; local chiefs could not suppress them.
idiomatic: Brigands rose in Xihe and Jianxing, and local chiefs could not put them down.

literal: Taizong therefore summoned Xuanbo, Duke of Beixin An Tong, Marquis of Shouguang Sun Jian, Marquis of Yuancheng Yuan Qu and asked: "Earlier because violent ruffians disturbed the people we summoned them to the capital, yet the administrators failed in soothing them and many fled.
idiomatic: Taizong then called Xuanbo, Duke of Beixin An Tong, Marquis of Shouguang Sun Jian, and Marquis of Yuancheng Yuan Qu and asked: "We summoned violent men to the capital because they troubled the people, yet the magistrates failed to soothe them and many fled.

literal: Now offenders are many and cannot all be executed; I wish a great amnesty to relieve this — what do you think?
idiomatic: Now the guilty are many and cannot all be killed; I wish a great amnesty to ease the matter — what do you say?

literal: " Qu replied: "If people flee without crime yet you pardon anyway, it seems as though the throne is begging those below; better first execute the chief evildoers and pardon their followers.
idiomatic: " Qu answered: "If men flee though guiltless and you pardon all the same, it will look as if the throne begs its subjects. Better execute the ringleaders first and pardon the rest.

literal: " Xuanbo said: "A king governs all under Heaven with settling the people as root — how can he mind small bends of right and wrong.
idiomatic: " Xuanbo said: "A king rules the world with the people's peace as his root — he cannot fuss over small twists of right and wrong.

literal: If zither and lute are out of tune, they must be restrung;
idiomatic: When zither and lute are out of tune, they must be restrung;

literal: if laws are uneven, they must be swept away and remade.
idiomatic: when laws lean awry, they must be cleared away and set anew.

literal: Amnesty is not the straight path, yet may be used as expedient; from Qin and Han onward none failed to follow in succession.
idiomatic: Amnesty is not the straight road, yet may serve as expedient; from Qin and Han on none failed to use it in turn.

literal: Qu's words — execute first then pardon — meet at being unable to do both; which is better than one act to settle matters.
idiomatic: Qu's plan — kill first, pardon after — cannot do both; better one stroke to settle the affair.

literal: If after pardon they still do not reform, execution is not too late.
idiomatic: If after pardon they still do not mend, execution will not be too late.

literal: " Taizong followed this.
idiomatic: " Taizong took his counsel.

literal: At the beginning of the Shenrui era he ordered Xuanbo with Duke of Nanping Song and others to sit to the right of the carriage-halting gate and manage myriad state affairs.
idiomatic: At the opening of the Shenrui era he ordered Xuanbo with Duke of Nanping Song and others to sit right of the carriage-halting gate and handle the weight of state.

literal: Tens of thousands of Hu households in Bingzhou raided south into the interior riverlands; General Gongsun Biao and others led troops against them and were defeated.
idiomatic: Tens of thousands of Hu households in Bingzhou raided south into the inner riverlands; General Gongsun Biao and others marched against them and were beaten.

literal: Taizong asked the assembled ministers: "The Hu raiders run wild and their numbers are not few; Biao and the rest cannot control them.
idiomatic: Taizong asked the ministers: "The Hu run wild and their numbers are great; Biao and his command cannot hold them.

literal: If we do not strike early the good people will suffer great harm.
idiomatic: If we do not strike soon the good people will suffer deeply.

literal: Now it is deep autumn — we cannot for small bandits again raise hosts and abandon the people's livelihood.
idiomatic: Yet it is deep autumn — we cannot for small bandits raise great armies again and ruin the people's harvest.

literal: What is to be done?
idiomatic: What is to be done? (record).

literal: " Xuanbo replied: "Biao's armies are not insufficient, but they failed in disposition, so the small bandits gained a breathing space.
idiomatic: " Xuanbo answered: "Biao's forces were not too few; they failed in deployment, and so the small bandits caught their breath.

literal: Though the Hu masses are large they have no fierce chief commander — as the saying goes, a thousand slaves share one gallbladder.
idiomatic: Though the Hu are many, they have no bold master to lead them — as the proverb says, a thousand slaves share one gut.
